summary: Defines extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol that support the procedures of the Hierarchical PCE architecture from RFC 6805. This hierarchy lets path computation find good end-to-end paths across multiple domains.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8685 defines how a parent path computation server and a child one talk to each other. The child handles the domain it knows, and asks the parent for the plan that crosses several domains. The RFC adds the new messages, fields and error codes that the two need, so that a path from one corner of a network to another can be worked out when no single server can see the whole topology.

subtitle: The PCEP messages and fields that let a parent path computation server and its child servers plan one route across several network domains.

tldr.problem: A route that crosses several domains, such as IGP areas or autonomous systems, cannot be computed by one server that only sees its own domain, and the Hierarchical PCE architecture of RFC 6805 had no protocol encoding.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8685 adds new TLVs, objective function codes, metric types, an SVEC flag, an error type and NO-PATH flags to PCEP, so a child PCE can ask a parent PCE for a domain sequence or a full end-to-end path.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that gives H-PCE a wire format. It has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8685 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It is not obsoleted, so it remains the definition of the H-PCE PCEP extensions together with that update.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) gives Path Computation Elements (PCEs) and Path Computation Clients (PCCs) a way to exchange path computation requests and the paths computed for them.

The ability to compute the routes of end-to-end inter-domain MPLS Traffic Engineering and GMPLS label switched paths is expressed as requirements in RFC 4105 and RFC 4216, and it may be realized by a PCE. The methods for establishing and controlling such paths are documented in RFC 4726.

RFC 6805 describes a Hierarchical Path Computation Element (H-PCE) architecture for computing end-to-end paths for inter-domain MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs. In that architecture, the parent PCE computes a multi-domain path from the domain connectivity information, and a child PCE, which may be responsible for one or several domains, computes the intra-domain path from its own domain topology information.

This document defines the PCEP extensions needed to implement the H-PCE procedures described in RFC 6805.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP is how a client asks a path computer for a route and receives the answer. Some routes have to cross several network domains, and no single path computer can see them all. The hierarchical arrangement puts a parent path computer above child ones, so that the parent can plan across domains while each child plans inside its own.

sections.title: The Path Computation Procedure
sections.content:
The RFC lists the end-to-end domain path computation procedure of the H-PCE architecture in eight steps.

  1. A PCC sends the inter-domain Path Computation Request messages to the child PCE responsible for its domain.
  2. The child PCE forwards the request to the parent PCE.
  3. The parent PCE computes the likely domain paths from the ingress domain to the egress domain.
  4. The parent PCE sends the intra-domain PCReq messages, between the domain border nodes, to the child PCEs responsible for the domains along the domain path.
  5. The child PCEs return the intra-domain paths to the parent PCE.
  6. The parent PCE constructs the end-to-end inter-domain path from the intra-domain paths.
  7. The parent PCE returns the inter-domain path to the child PCE.
  8. The child PCE forwards the inter-domain path to the PCC.

The parent PCE may also be asked for only the sequence of domains, which lets the child use other inter-domain procedures, such as per-domain path computation of RFC 5152 or the backward-recursive procedure of RFC 5441.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent path computer works in two stages. First it works out which domains the path has to pass through, then it asks each child path computer in turn for the path inside its domain. When all the answers arrive, the parent joins them into one end-to-end path and hands it back down to the client.

sections.title: What the Document Leaves Out
sections.content:
Several functions are out of scope. Determining the destination domain is not covered, whether it is done from reachability information collected from child domains, by asking the child PCEs whether they hold the destination node, or by any other method. The methods for the parent's traffic engineering database are not covered either, though suitable mechanisms include YANG-based management interfaces, BGP-LS of RFC 7752 and future extensions to PCEP. Learning the domain connectivity and the border node addresses is also out of scope, with the same list of candidate mechanisms.

Stateful PCE operations are out of scope as well, and so is the applicability of the H-PCE model to large multi-domain environments. The hierarchical relationship model of RFC 6805 applies to environments with small groups of domains where the visibility from the ingress label switching routers is limited. As RFC 7399 points out, applying the H-PCE model to very large groups of domains, such as the Internet, is not considered feasible or desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not decide how the parent finds out which domains exist or which border nodes they have, and it does not cover stateful path computers. It also says the hierarchy is for small groups of domains. The whole Internet is not a realistic case for this model.

sections.title: The New TLVs
sections.content:
Two new TLVs are carried in the OPEN object, so that the capability and the domain information can be advertised when the session is set up. A third TLV is carried in the Request Parameters object.

The H-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV has type 13 and a fixed length of 4 octets. Its value is a 32-bit flags field with one flag defined: the P bit, the Parent PCE Request bit. When it is set, the speaker wants its peer to act as a parent PCE. A child PCE must include this TLV and set the P flag, and a parent PCE must include it and leave the flag clear. In a client to child PCE relationship, neither side sets the flag. If both peers set it, the session establishment must fail, and the speaker must respond with a PCEP error message using Error-Type 1, PCEP session establishment failure. If a PCE understands the H-PCE request but did not advertise the capability, it must send a PCEP error with Error-Type 28, H-PCE error, and Error-Value 1, H-PCE capability not advertised.

The Domain-ID TLV has type 14 and a variable length. Its value carries a Domain Type of 8 bits, a reserved field, and the Domain ID. Four domain types are defined: type 1 carries a 2-byte AS number padded to a 4-byte boundary, type 2 a 4-byte AS number, type 3 a 4-byte OSPF area ID, and type 4 a 2-byte Area-Len with a variable-length IS-IS area ID, padded to a 4-byte boundary. When a PCE serves more than one domain, several Domain-ID TLVs are included.

The H-PCE-FLAG TLV has type 15 and a fixed length of 4 octets. Its 32-bit flags field carries two bits: the D bit, the Disallow Domain Re-entry bit, which signals that the computed path does not enter a domain more than once, and the S bit, the Domain Sequence bit, which signals that the child PCE wants only the domain sequence in the reply. The presence of the TLV indicates that H-PCE-based path computation is being requested.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces of information are added to the signalling. One says that a peer is to act as a parent path computer. One names the domains a path computer serves, with four ways of writing a domain identifier. One tells the parent what the child wants: a full path, or only the list of domains, and whether a domain may be entered twice.

sections.title: Objective Functions and Metrics
sections.content:
Three objective functions are defined for the H-PCE model. MTD, Minimize the number of Transit Domains, has OF code 12 and finds a path that passes through the fewest transit domains. MBN, Minimize the number of Border Nodes, has OF code 13 and finds a path that passes through the fewest border nodes, where a border node is counted for each place where consecutive links belong to different domains. MCTD, Minimize the number of Common Transit Domains, has OF code 14 and finds a set of paths that share as few transit domains as possible. Domain diversity is the reason that objective function exists: a pair of paths is domain-diverse when they do not transit any of the same domains, and the point is to avoid fate-sharing, or to avoid specific transit domains for security, geopolitical or commercial reasons.

The OF object may carry an OF-List TLV, which allows several OF codes to be encoded. Only the first code in the list is considered, and the parent PCE must use that code in the intra-domain request it sends to the child PCE. The code inside the OF object must be one of the H-PCE codes, and the code in the list must not be one, otherwise the speaker must respond with Error-Type 10, reception of an invalid object, and Error-Value 23, incompatible OF codes in H-PCE.

Two metric types are added to the METRIC object: T=20, the Domain Count metric, which is the number of domains crossed, and T=21, the Border Node Count metric, which is the number of border nodes. A re-entered domain is counted twice. A client or child PCE can use either metric to put a bound on the inter-domain path, with the B bit set, or to ask for it to be optimized, with the B flag cleared and the C flag set. The parent PCE can also send the metric back with a NO-PATH object when it cannot meet the constraint.

The SVEC object gains a Domain Diverse O-bit, number 18. When it is set, the computed paths must not have any transit domains in common. The other SVEC bits, for link, node and shared-risk diversity, may still be set and must still be applied inside the shared ingress and egress domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent can be told what kind of path to look for: one that crosses as few other domains as possible, one that passes through as few border routers as possible, or, when several paths are computed together, one set that avoids sharing transit domains. Two measurements go with them, the number of domains crossed and the number of border nodes, and a client can put a limit on either.

sections.title: The Session and Request Procedures
sections.content:
If a child PCE wants to use its peer as a parent, it must set the P flag in the H-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV inside the OPEN object of the Open message during session initialization. The child PCE may also report its list of domain identifiers to the parent with Domain-ID TLVs in the same OPEN object. The OF codes of this document can be carried in the OF-List TLV of the OPEN object, which means that the PCE can implement those objective functions; a child PCE can use that information when it needs to choose a parent PCE for a request with a particular objective function.

When a child PCE sends a PCReq to a peer that requires parental activity, and the capability TLV was not taken into account during session establishment, the peer should send a PCEP error with Error-Type 28 and Error-Value 1, H-PCE capability not advertised. When a peer does not want to act as the parent for a particular child, it should send Error-Type 28 with Error-Value 2, parent PCE capability cannot be provided.

If a child PCE only wants the domain sequence, it sets the domain path request bit in the H-PCE-FLAG TLV in the RP object of the PCReq. The parent PCE then computes a domain sequence rather than an end-to-end path, and on success returns it in the Explicit Route Object of the PCRep. If the computation fails, it sends a PCReq carrying the NO-PATH object.
sections.plainLanguage: The relationship is set up when the session starts: the child asks to be served by the parent, and may list the domains it covers. If a request then needs the parent and the parent never agreed to the role, the request is refused with an error that says which of the two cases it was. The child can also ask for only the sequence of domains, which is then returned in the route object of the reply.

sections.title: Why a Path Cannot Be Found
sections.content:
A PCE that can act as a parent may not be configured or willing to act as the parent for a particular child, in which case a PCEP error message with the H-PCE Error-Type 28 and an applicable Error-Value results.

The parent PCE may also fail to find the multi-domain path or the domain sequence for several reasons: a child PCE cannot find a suitable path to the egress, the parent does not hear from a child PCE for a specified time, or the objective functions in the request cannot be met. In that case the parent may send a negative reply with the NO-PATH object, and an extension to that object carries the reason.

Four new flags in the NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV carry those reasons. Bit 22 means the destination domain is unknown, bit 21 that one or more child PCEs are unresponsive, bit 20 that no resources are available in one or more domains, and bit 19 that the destination is not found in the indicated domain.
sections.plainLanguage: When no path can be found, the reply says why. Four reasons have their own flag: the destination domain is unknown, a child path computer did not answer, there is no capacity in one of the domains, or the destination is not in the domain the request named.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The H-PCE procedure relies on PCEP and inherits the security considerations of RFC 5440. Since PCEP runs over TCP, it can also use TCP security mechanisms such as the TCP Authentication Option of RFC 5925 or Transport Layer Security.

Any multi-domain operation involves exchanging information across domain boundaries, which may be a significant security and confidentiality risk, especially when the child domains are controlled by different commercial interests. PCEP lets individual PCEs keep their domain path information confidential by using path-keys, and the H-PCE architecture is designed to isolate as much information about domain topology and capabilities as possible.

On the management side, the RFC notes that a parent PCE must only accept requests from authorized child PCEs and should drop requests from unauthorized ones, which means it must be able to cryptographically authenticate them. Multi-party shared key schemes are not recommended for inter-domain relationships, because of the risk of impersonation and repudiation and the operational difficulty of revocation. Discovery of the parent and child relationships is not part of the architecture, because mechanisms that advertise or query PCE locations across domain or provider boundaries are undesirable for security, scaling, commercial and confidentiality reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: Each child path computer is configured with the address of its parent, and the parent only accepts requests from children it has authorized. Sharing a key between several parties is discouraged, because a revocation then affects everyone. The relationships are configured rather than discovered, so that path computer locations are not advertised across provider boundaries.
